notes.meaning: It was the same busy day as the teaching and arguments in chapter 12. Jesus did not stop to rest. He kept on doing good. He left the house, which was probably Peter's home, and sat by the Sea of Galilee.

The crowd was so big that Jesus got into a boat. That way He was not crushed, and people could see and hear Him better. Sitting was the normal way a Jewish teacher taught. Matthew Henry notes that Jesus did not need a grand building. He used whatever place God gave Him.

A parable is a story from everyday life. It is set beside a spiritual truth to help us understand that truth. Jesus begins with a farmer scattering seed, a sight everyone knew. The sower stands for Christ, who sows in person or through those who preach His word. Most parables make one main point, so we should not press every small detail.

Some seed landed on the hard, beaten path beside the field. The plough had never broken up that ground, so the seed just lay on top. The birds quickly ate it. Wesley notes that Jesus lists the dangers to the seed in the order they happen.

Rocky ground means a thin layer of soil lying over rock. The seed came up fast because there was little earth to cover it. The shallow soil that made it sprout so quickly is the same thing that would soon kill it.

When the hot sun came out, the young plants dried up. Their roots could not reach down for water. Matthew Henry says the scorching sun stands for trouble and persecution. The same sun that helps a well-rooted plant grow burns up one with no root.
This part of the field had been ploughed, but the thorns had never been cleared out. Their roots were already in the soil. They grew up alongside the grain, crowded it, and slowly choked it to death.

Good soil is soft, deep and free of thorns. Seed there grows into a real harvest. A crop of a hundred times what was planted is not an exaggeration. Isaac reaped that much in Genesis 26:12. The yields differ, but every part of the good soil bears fruit.
This was a common saying meaning "Pay attention!" Jesus wanted people to think hard about what He had said. Calvin adds that it also shows not everyone truly hears. It is the Lord who opens ears.

This seems to be the first time Jesus taught mainly in parables, and the disciples were puzzled. They asked partly because they cared whether the crowd would understand. Matthew Henry says we too should care that others are helped by God's word, not just ourselves.

In the Bible, a "mystery" is not something no one can understand. It is a truth God kept hidden for a long time and has now made known. Understanding these truths about God's kingdom was a gift given to the disciples. The crowd had not received it. Such knowledge comes from God, not from our own cleverness.

differ.view: Understanding and faith are given only to the elect (the people God has freely chosen). The rest are left blind by God's just judgment.
God gives this knowledge to those He has chosen, and not because they are better than others. When people are passed by, it is because of their own sin.
The knowledge is given to those who use the grace they already have. It is never God's will that keeps people from it, only their own stubbornness.

notes.meaning: People who value and use the light God gives them will be given more. People who neglect it will lose even what little they seem to have. Moral strength works the same way: it grows when used and fades when it is not.

differ.view: Here the saying mainly praises God's kindness. He keeps adding to what He has begun in His own people. In Matthew 25 the same words are used about the right use of gifts.
"Whoever has" means whoever puts God's grace to use. This is God's fixed rule in dealing with everyone.

notes.meaning: The crowd saw Jesus' miracles and heard His words, yet they did not really take them in. They had shut their eyes to His plain teaching, so now He spoke in pictures. Even so, a parable could still stir a person to ask and search for its meaning.

Isaiah 6:9-10 described the people of his own day. It was being fulfilled again in Jesus' time. Their hearts had grown "fat" and dull. They closed their own eyes because they did not want to see their need and turn to God. God in fairness let their chosen blindness stand. "Heal" here means to forgive and save.

The disciples were blessed because their eyes and ears were open to the truth. This was a gift of God's grace. They saw God's glory in Jesus and knew Him as the Savior. Calvin adds that believers in every age share this kind of seeing through the gospel.

Prophets and godly people of the Old Testament longed to see the promised Messiah, God's chosen King. They saw only hints and shadows, because God's time had not yet come. So the disciples were favored even above those great saints. Those who live after Christ have reason to be very thankful.

Jesus now explains the story to His disciples. The word "you" is stressed: the meaning held back from others is given to them. Mark shows this parable is a key to understanding the others. Matthew Henry notes it is good to go over again what we have heard.

The seed is God's word about His kingdom. The path is a careless listener who does not take the message to heart. Satan, the evil one, is like the birds. He snatches the word away before it can take root, sometimes through distracting thoughts or people who change the subject. We guard against this by preparing our hearts and holding onto the word with thought and prayer.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Chrysostom stresses that the blame lies with the listener's choice, not their nature. It rests with us whether the seed is taken away.

notes.meaning: This listener gets excited and receives the word quickly and gladly. But they take it in without thinking it through. Many enjoy a good sermon yet are not truly changed by it. The quick start looks better at first than the slower growth in good soil.

This person has no deep root. They have never truly seen their own sin and their need for Christ. When trouble or persecution comes because of their faith, they stumble and fall away. The hard times show what was really there, just as hot sun shows how shallow the soil is.

Here the word is not rejected outright. It is slowly crowded out. Worries about daily life and the false promises of money act like thorns that choke it. Money is called "deceitful" because it promises happiness it cannot give. The danger grows when we put our trust in it. Wesley puts it this way: worries are thorns for the poor, and wealth is the thorn for the rich.

differ.view: True faith, planted by God's Spirit, can never be lost. So those who fall away only seemed to believe.
This hearer did have root and was in large part changed inside. Yet the thorns slowly choked the word until it bore no fruit.

notes.meaning: Good soil is the person who hears the word, takes it to heart, and lives it out. Fruit is what marks true believers from those who only appear to believe. Good soil is not free of every stone or thorn, but none stop it from bearing fruit. Some bear more than others. We should aim high, yet not look down on those who bear less.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern critics think the explanation in verses 18-23 reads the story with too much detail. They doubt it is exactly what Jesus first said.

notes.meaning: Here "the kingdom of heaven" means God's work through the gospel in this present age, including the church on earth. The man who sows good seed is Christ. He sows only what is good.

While people slept, an enemy secretly sowed weeds among the wheat. The weed was probably darnel, which looks just like wheat while it is young. The enemy is the devil, who works in the dark and hides himself. He could just walk away. Sin grows easily on its own, while good seed needs constant care.

At first the weeds could not be told apart from the wheat. Only when the grain began to form did they show up. In the same way, real faith and false faith are known not by talk or outward show, but by fruit.

The servants stand for Christ's ministers. They are surprised and troubled to find false believers mixed into the church. The master had sown good seed. Whatever is wrong in the church does not come from Christ.

"An enemy did this." God did not plant evil; the devil did, with people going along with him. The master does not blame his faithful servants. The servants want to pull the weeds right away. That shows the kind of hasty zeal James and John showed when they wanted to call down fire from heaven.

The master says no, because pulling weeds would tear up the wheat too. No one can perfectly tell true believers from false ones. Christ would rather let some weeds stay than harm His wheat. Open and serious wrongdoing in the church should still be dealt with, but with great care and gentleness. The final sorting waits for the harvest.
